results.summary: This is a two-channel 8-bit single-slope ramp ADC built from analog blocks including a bias generator, linear ramp, 2:1 transmission-gate MUX, sample-and-hold, and a two-stage comparator. The selected input is compared against an on-chip ramp, and the 8-bit count at the first crossing is latched and presented on uo_out, with a sample-valid pulse on uio_out[0]. It needs an external clock around 4 MHz, a 0 to 1 V analog signal on ua[0] or ua[1], logic inputs for channel select and sample-and-hold bypass, and a logic analyzer or read-back on the digital outputs. The documentation is brief and does not report measured silicon results, so the actual reference value and temperature behavior are only expected rather than confirmed.

This is a Brokaw bandgap voltage reference built with SKY130 PNP BJTs, using a PTAT current generator and a summing amplifier with OTA feedback to produce a stable reference near 1.2 V. The circuit includes a bias generator, a ramp generator, and a 2:1 analog MUX, with the output available on ua[0] and ua[1]. It requires an external clock and a 0 to 1 V analog input, and the digital output is read via uo_out. The documentation is brief and does not report measured silicon results, so the actual reference value and temperature behavior are only expected rather than confirmed.

This is a random delay generator that produces a variable delay based on an internal random or pseudo-random process. It uses a button input to trigger the delay and outputs a pulse on an LED or buzzer after the delay period. The documentation is short and does not describe the internal timing or random-delay implementation in detail. It is likely intended for educational or game-like applications where unpredictable timing is desired.

This is a RISC-V CPU core designed for educational purposes, featuring an ALU, barrel shifter, comparator, and branch prediction logic. It is implemented in Verilog and intended to be used as a learning tool for computer architecture. The design is synthesized for the Tiny Tapeout platform and can be tested with standard RISC-V programs. The documentation is brief but indicates a full processor implementation.

This is a RISC-V CPU core with a branch predictor, designed for educational purposes. It includes an ALU, comparator, and finite state machine control logic. The design is implemented in Verilog and targets the Tiny Tapeout platform. It is intended to demonstrate advanced CPU features like branch prediction in a simple, learnable format.

This is a machine learning accelerator that uses a systolic array for neural network inference. It includes a multiplier and DSP blocks to perform matrix operations. The design is implemented in Verilog and targets the Tiny Tapeout platform. It is intended for edge AI applications, though the documentation is sparse.

This is a cellular automaton display that generates patterns on a VGA output. It uses a PRNG to seed the automaton and displays the evolving patterns on a screen. The design is implemented in Verilog and targets the Tiny Tapeout platform. It is intended for visual demos or educational purposes.

This is a systolic array accelerator that drives a VGA display to show visual patterns. It includes a graphics output and uses a PRNG for pattern generation. The design is implemented in Verilog and targets the Tiny Tapeout platform. It is intended for demoscene-style visual showcases.

This is a pattern generator that produces visual patterns on a VGA output. The documentation is very thin, providing no detail on the pattern generation, resolution, or any configurable inputs. It is implemented in Verilog and targets the Tiny Tapeout platform. The design likely outputs simple geometric or test patterns for display.

This is an esoteric computing design that outputs to a VGA display. It uses a systolic array for computation and generates graphics output. The design is implemented in Verilog and targets the Tiny Tapeout platform. The documentation is sparse, but it appears to be a novelty or artistic project.
